description: Decision tree from study design to statistical test. Each node is a question; option.to is another node id, or L:<test_id> for a test in tests.

status_levels.ready: One scipy or statsmodels call. Safe to automate.
status_levels.helper: No single call. Needs a small function or another package.
status_levels.judgment: Modeling decisions the pipeline should not make alone.

root.q: What are you trying to find out?
root.help: Pick the closest match. You can step back to any earlier answer.

opts.label: How one outcome differs or depends on something
opts.sub: Group comparisons, regression, survival. One outcome variable.

opts.label: How several outcomes differ together
opts.sub: Two or more outcome variables analyzed jointly.

opts.label: Whether two variables are related
opts.sub: Correlation or association, with no outcome–predictor split.

opts.label: How well raters, methods, or a diagnostic test agree
opts.sub: Reliability, method comparison, diagnostic accuracy.

out_type.q: What type is the outcome variable?
out_type.help: If a continuous measure was split into categories, choose continuous. Dichotomizing throws information away.

opts.label: Continuous
opts.sub: Measured on a scale: blood pressure, HbA1c, length of stay.

opts.label: Ordinal
opts.sub: Ordered categories: Likert items, tumor grade, pain scale.

opts.label: Binary
opts.sub: Two categories: readmitted or not, responder or not.

opts.label: Nominal, three or more categories
opts.sub: Unordered categories: discharge destination, disease subtype.

opts.label: Count
opts.sub: Number of events: ED visits per year, lesions per scan.

opts.label: Time to event
opts.sub: Time until an event happens, with some subjects censored.

cont_struct.help: This is the study-design axis. Treating paired or clustered data as independent makes standard errors too small.

opts.label: Independent
opts.sub: Each subject contributes one measurement.

opts.label: Paired or matched
opts.sub: Two measurements per subject, or matched pairs.

opts.label: Repeated or clustered
opts.sub: Three or more measurements per subject, or subjects nested in sites.

cont_ind.help: A grouping variable is a categorical predictor, such as treatment arm.

opts.label: None, compare with a reference value
opts.sub: A target, a norm, or a historical mean.

opts.label: One grouping variable, three or more groups
Two or more grouping variables
opts.sub: For example treatment × sex, including the interaction.

opts.label: Several predictors, or groups plus covariates
opts.sub: Multiple regression, or ANCOVA.

cont_rep.q: What does the repeated structure look like?
cont_rep.help: Most clinical longitudinal data has missing visits, which usually points to a mixed model.

opts.label: One within-subject factor, every subject complete
opts.sub: Same time points for everyone, no missing data.

opts.label: Missing visits, uneven timing, between-subject factors, or nesting
You want population-averaged effects
opts.sub: The average effect across the population, not per subject.

opts.sub: Each subject contributes one measurement.

opts.sub: Same subjects measured twice, or matched pairs.

opts.label: Three or more conditions per subject, complete data
Clustered or longitudinal, with covariates
opts.sub: Patients within clinics, visits within patients.

opts.label: None, compare with a reference proportion
One grouping variable, three or more groups

Independent

count_ind.q: What do you need to do with the counts?
count_ind.help: Follow-up time usually differs between subjects. Model it as exposure rather than ignoring it.

opts.label: Compare event rates between two groups
Model counts with predictors
opts.sub: Optionally with follow-up time as an exposure offset.

opts.label: Far more zeros than expected
opts.sub: Some subjects may never be at risk, such as never-users.

surv.q: What do you need from the survival analysis?
surv.help: Censoring is what makes this survival data. If everyone was followed until the event, a continuous-outcome method may do.

opts.label: Compare survival between groups
opts.sub: No adjustment for covariates.

opts.label: Estimate hazard ratios, adjusted for covariates
More than one event type can end follow-up
opts.sub: For example death before readmission.

opts.label: Subjects nested in sites, or a covariate breaks proportional hazards

mv.q: What do you want to do with the outcomes?
mv.help: If the several outcomes are one measure taken at several times, go back and choose one outcome with a repeated structure.

opts.label: Compare groups on them
opts.sub: Several continuous outcomes, such as a panel of related labs.

opts.label: Measure an underlying construct
opts.sub: The outcomes are items of a scale or questionnaire.

assoc.q: What kinds of variables are they?
assoc.help: Correlation describes association. To check whether two methods agree, go back and choose agreement.

opts.label: Two continuous, adjusting for other variables
Three or more raters, categorical ratings
Two methods measuring the same continuous quantity
opts.sub: A new device against a reference method.

opts.label: Reliability of continuous ratings
opts.sub: Across raters, or test–retest.

opts.label: A binary test against a gold standard
A continuous score against a gold standard
opts.sub: A biomarker, or a model's predicted probability.

one_sample_t.name: One-sample t-test
one_sample_t.when: Compare the mean of one continuous measure with a fixed reference value: a norm, a target, or a historical mean.

checks.t: Values roughly normal (matters less above about 30 subjects)
No extreme outliers driving the mean

fb.t: Wilcoxon signed-rank against the reference value.

cross.c: sm.stats.DescrStatsW(x).ttest_mean(mu0)
cross.why: Same test in a second library. The t statistic and p-value should match to many decimals.

one_sample_t.report: Mean difference with 95% CI; Cohen's d = (mean − μ₀) / SD.

indep_t.name: Independent-samples t-test (Welch)
indep_t.when: Compare the means of a continuous outcome between two independent groups.

checks.t: Each group roughly normal
One measurement per subject, no matching between groups
Unequal variances are fine: Welch doesn't assume them equal

fb.t: Mann–Whitney U.

cross.c:
from statsmodels.stats.weightstats import ttest_ind
ttest_ind(g1, g2, usevar='unequal')
cross.why: Same Welch test in statsmodels. Statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value should match.

indep_t.report: Mean difference with 95% CI; Hedges' g.
indep_t.watch: Don't choose between Student's and Welch's test from a Levene p-value. Welch costs almost nothing when variances are equal.

oneway_anova.name: One-way ANOVA
oneway_anova.when: Compare a continuous outcome across three or more independent groups.

checks.t: Residuals roughly normal
Similar variances across groups; if not, use Welch's ANOVA

fb.t: Kruskal–Wallis if residuals aren't normal. Welch's ANOVA if only the variances differ.

oneway_anova.run:
stats.f_oneway(*groups)

# unequal variances
from statsmodels.stats.oneway import anova_oneway
anova_oneway(df['y'], groups=df['group'], use_var='unequal')

cross.c:
m = smf.ols('y ~ C(group)', df).fit()
sm.stats.anova_lm(m, typ=2)
cross.why: The regression framing gives the same F. It must equal scipy's.

oneway_anova.report: η² or ω² from the ANOVA table.
oneway_anova.post: Tukey HSD with statsmodels pairwise_tukeyhsd(df['y'], df['group']), cross-checked against scipy.stats.tukey_hsd.

factorial_anova.name: Factorial ANOVA
factorial_anova.when: Two or more grouping factors, such as treatment × sex, with a continuous outcome and their interaction.

checks.t: Residuals roughly normal
Similar variances across cells
Count subjects per cell. Unbalanced designs change the answer

fb.t: Heteroscedasticity-robust (HC3) standard errors, or a permutation test on the interaction. Rank-based ART has no maintained Python port.

factorial_anova.run:
m = smf.ols('y ~ C(a) * C(b)', df).fit()
sm.stats.anova_lm(m, typ=2)

cross.c:
# Type III needs sum-to-zero contrasts
m3 = smf.ols('y ~ C(a, Sum) * C(b, Sum)', df).fit()
sm.stats.anova_lm(m3, typ=3)
cross.why: In a balanced design Types II and III agree. If they don't, the design is unbalanced and you need to choose deliberately.

factorial_anova.report: Partial η² per effect; simple effects if the interaction matters.
factorial_anova.watch: The sums-of-squares type, and whether main effects mean anything under an interaction, are judgment calls. The tool should show both, not pick silently.

simple_lin_reg.name: Simple linear regression
simple_lin_reg.when: Model a continuous outcome as a linear function of one continuous predictor.

checks.t: Linear relationship: plot residuals against fitted values
Residuals roughly normal
Constant residual variance
checks.c:
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
het_breuschpagan(m.resid, m.model.exog)

checks.t: No single point dominating the fit

fb.t: Spearman correlation for a monotonic relationship, or HC3 standard errors for unequal variance.

cross.c:
m = smf.ols('y ~ x', df).fit()
m.params, m.pvalues
cross.why: Slope, intercept and p-value should match linregress exactly.

multiple_reg.name: Multiple linear regression / ANCOVA
multiple_reg.when: Continuous outcome with several predictors, or a group comparison adjusted for covariates (ANCOVA).

checks.t: Residuals roughly normal
Constant residual variance
Predictors not too collinear (VIF under about 5)
For ANCOVA, no group × covariate interaction

fb.t: Heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors: .fit(cov_type='HC3').

multiple_reg.run: m = smf.ols('y ~ C(group) + age + baseline', df).fit()

cross.c: np.linalg.lstsq(m.model.exog, m.model.endog, rcond=None)[0]
cross.why: A raw least-squares solve should reproduce m.params.

multiple_reg.report: Coefficients with 95% CI; adjusted R²; partial η² for the ANCOVA group effect.
multiple_reg.watch: The covariate list comes from the design spec, fixed before seeing results. The tool shouldn't choose it.

paired_t.name: Paired t-test
paired_t.when: Two measurements on the same subjects (pre and post, left and right) or matched pairs, with a continuous outcome.

checks.t: Differences roughly normal
Pairs joined on subject ID, never on row order

fb.t: Wilcoxon signed-rank on the paired differences.

cross.c: stats.ttest_1samp(after - before, 0)
cross.why: A paired t-test is a one-sample test on the differences. The result is identical.

paired_t.report: Mean difference with 95% CI; d_z = mean(diff) / SD(diff).

rm_anova.name: Repeated-measures ANOVA
rm_anova.when: Three or more measurements per subject on one within-subject factor, with every subject complete.

checks.t: Sphericity. Mauchly's test is in pingouin, not statsmodels
Every subject has every level
Residuals roughly normal

fb.t: Friedman test for non-normal data. A linear mixed model if any visits are missing.

rm_anova.run:
from statsmodels.stats.anova import AnovaRM
AnovaRM(df, depvar='y', subject='id', within=['time']).fit()

cross.c:
import pingouin as pg
pg.rm_anova(df, dv='y', within='time', subject='id', correction=True)
cross.why: The uncorrected F should match AnovaRM. pingouin adds the Greenhouse–Geisser correction that statsmodels lacks.

rm_anova.report: Partial or generalized η²; Greenhouse–Geisser p if sphericity fails.
rm_anova.watch: AnovaRM fails on missing cells. Missing visits are common in clinical data, which usually means a mixed model instead.

lmm.name: Linear mixed model
lmm.when: Repeated or clustered continuous outcomes with missing visits, uneven timing, between-subject factors, or nesting such as patients within sites.

checks.t: Random intercepts and slopes chosen from the design
Model converged without boundary warnings
Residuals roughly normal
Enough clusters to estimate the variance components

fb.t: A population-averaged GEE if the random-effects structure won't converge.

lmm.run:
m = smf.mixedlm('y ~ time * group', df, groups=df['id'],
                re_formula='~time').fit(reml=True)

cross.c:
g = smf.gee('y ~ time * group', 'id', df,
            cov_struct=sm.cov_struct.Exchangeable()).fit()
cross.why: With an identity link, mixed-model fixed effects and GEE estimates target similar quantities. Large disagreement is a warning about the model, not rounding.

lmm.report: Fixed effects with 95% CI; variance components; ICC.
lmm.watch: Random-effects structure, REML versus ML for model comparison, and how time is coded are modeling decisions. This is the core of the tail that needs a person.

gee_cont.name: GEE for a continuous outcome
gee_cont.when: Clustered or longitudinal continuous data where you want population-averaged effects rather than subject-specific ones.

checks.t: Enough clusters. Robust standard errors get unreliable below about 40
Working correlation chosen: exchangeable, AR(1), or independence
Missing data plausibly completely at random

fb.t: Linear mixed model.

cross.c:
smf.gee('y ~ time * group', 'id', df,
        family=sm.families.Gaussian(),
        cov_struct=sm.cov_struct.Independence()).fit()
cross.why: Robust standard errors should be similar across working correlations. Big swings mean the estimate is fragile.

gee_cont.report: Coefficients with robust 95% CI; QIC to compare working correlations.
gee_cont.watch: GEE assumes data are missing completely at random; mixed models tolerate missing at random. With dropout, that difference matters.

wilcoxon_signed.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired)
wilcoxon_signed.when: Paired or matched measurements when the differences aren't normal, or the outcome is ordinal.

checks.t: Differences roughly symmetric around their median
Decide how zero differences are handled

fb.t: Sign test, if the differences are clearly skewed.

cross.c:
d = after - before
stats.binomtest(int((d > 0).sum()), int((d != 0).sum()))
cross.why: The sign test has less power but should point the same way. If it doesn't, look at the distribution of differences.

wilcoxon_signed.report: Hodges–Lehmann median difference; matched-pairs rank-biserial correlation.

friedman.name: Friedman test
friedman.when: Three or more repeated conditions per subject with an ordinal or non-normal outcome and complete data.

checks.t: Every subject measured under every condition

fb.t: Ordinal GEE if the data are incomplete.

cross.c:
import pingouin as pg
pg.friedman(df, dv='y', within='time', subject='id')
cross.why: Same statistic. pingouin also reports Kendall's W.

friedman.post: Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction: statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests(p, method='holm').

ordinal_gee.name: Ordinal GEE
ordinal_gee.when: An ordinal outcome measured repeatedly or within clusters, with covariates.

checks.t: Proportional odds plausible, as for ordinal logistic regression
Enough clusters for robust standard errors
Every outcome level reasonably populated

fb.t: Collapse to binary and use logistic GEE, accepting the information loss.

cross.c:
# ignore clustering to see the naive estimate
from statsmodels.miscmodels.ordinal_model import OrderedModel
OrderedModel.from_formula('y ~ 0 + time + group', df,
                          distr='logit').fit(method='bfgs')
cross.why: Point estimates should agree in direction. The naive standard errors will be too small.

ordinal_gee.report: Cumulative odds ratios with robust 95% CI.

one_sample_wilcoxon.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank (one sample)
one_sample_wilcoxon.when: Compare the center of one ordinal or non-normal measure with a reference value.

checks.t: Distribution roughly symmetric around its median

fb.t: Sign test if the distribution is skewed.

cross.c: stats.binomtest(int((x > m0).sum()), int((x != m0).sum()))
cross.why: The sign test should agree in direction. Disagreement points to asymmetry.

mann_whitney.name: Mann–Whitney U test
mann_whitney.when: Two independent groups with an ordinal outcome, or a continuous outcome that isn't normal.

checks.t: Similar distribution shapes if you want to talk about medians. Otherwise it tests stochastic dominance

fb.t: Brunner–Munzel test when the group spreads differ a lot.

cross.c: stats.ranksums(g1, g2)
cross.why: The rank-sum test is the same test with a normal approximation. p-values should be close in moderate samples.

mann_whitney.report: Rank-biserial correlation, or the common-language effect size U / (n₁n₂).
mann_whitney.watch: U / (n₁n₂) is exactly the AUC. The same machinery powers the ROC leaf.

kruskal.name: Kruskal–Wallis test
kruskal.when: Three or more independent groups with an ordinal or non-normal continuous outcome.

checks.t: Similar distribution shapes if you want to talk about medians

cross.c:
# one-way ANOVA on ranks
r = stats.rankdata(df['y'])
stats.f_oneway(*[r[df['group'] == k] for k in df['group'].unique()])
cross.why: ANOVA on ranks approximates Kruskal–Wallis. It should agree on direction and roughly on p.

kruskal.post: Dunn's test with scikit_posthocs.posthoc_dunn(df, val_col='y', group_col='group', p_adjust='holm').

spearman.name: Spearman rank correlation
spearman.when: Monotonic association between two ordinal or non-normal continuous variables.

checks.t: Monotonic, not U-shaped. Plot it first

fb.t: Kendall's τ for small samples or many ties.

cross.c: stats.pearsonr(stats.rankdata(x), stats.rankdata(y))
cross.why: Spearman's ρ is Pearson's r on ranks. The coefficients must match exactly.

spearman.report: ρ with 95% CI (bootstrap or Fisher z).

ordinal_logit.name: Ordinal logistic regression
ordinal_logit.when: An ordinal outcome with several predictors and independent observations.

checks.t: Proportional odds. There's no built-in Brant test, so compare binary fits across cut-points
Every outcome level has enough observations

fb.t: Multinomial logistic regression if proportional odds clearly fails.

ordinal_logit.run:
from statsmodels.miscmodels.ordinal_model import OrderedModel
m = OrderedModel.from_formula('y ~ 0 + x1 + x2', df, distr='logit')
res = m.fit(method='bfgs')

cross.c:
# rough proportional-odds check
for cut in cut_points:
    d = df.assign(b=(df['y'] > cut).astype(int))
    print(cut, smf.logit('b ~ x1 + x2', d).fit(disp=0).params)
cross.why: Slopes should be roughly constant across cut-points. If they drift, proportional odds is doubtful.

mcnemar.name: McNemar's test
mcnemar.when: A binary outcome measured twice on the same subjects, or in matched pairs.

checks.t: A 2×2 table of paired outcomes, not two sets of marginal counts
Use the exact version when discordant pairs are few (under 25)

mcnemar.run:
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar
mcnemar(table, exact=True)

cross.c:
b, c = table[0][1], table[1][0]
stats.binomtest(b, b + c, 0.5)
cross.why: Exact McNemar is a binomial test on the discordant pairs. The p-value is identical.

mcnemar.report: Paired odds ratio b / c with CI; difference in proportions.

cochran_q.name: Cochran's Q test
cochran_q.when: A binary outcome under three or more conditions on the same subjects, with complete data.

checks.t: Every subject observed under every condition

fb.t: Logistic GEE for incomplete or clustered data.

cochran_q.run:
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import cochrans_q
cochrans_q(x)  # x: subjects × conditions, 0/1

cross.c:
import pingouin as pg
pg.cochran(df, dv='y', within='cond', subject='id')
cross.why: Second implementation. Q and p should match.

cochran_q.post: Pairwise McNemar tests with Holm correction.

gee_logit.name: Logistic GEE
gee_logit.when: A binary outcome measured repeatedly or within clusters, such as patients within clinics, with covariates.

checks.t: Enough clusters for robust standard errors
Working correlation chosen
Population-averaged rather than subject-specific effects are what you want

fb.t: A mixed-effects logistic model for subject-specific effects. statsmodels only has a Bayesian version (BinomialBayesMixedGLM).

cross.c:
smf.gee('y ~ time + group', 'id', df,
        family=sm.families.Binomial(),
        cov_struct=sm.cov_struct.Independence()).fit()
cross.why: Robust standard errors should be stable across working correlations.

binom_test.name: Exact binomial test
binom_test.when: Compare one observed proportion with a reference proportion.

checks.t: Independent trials, one per subject

cross.c:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import binom_test
binom_test(k, n, prop=p0)
cross.why: Same exact test in a second library.

two_by_two.name: Chi-square or Fisher's exact (2×2)
two_by_two.when: A binary outcome compared between two independent groups.

checks.t: Use Fisher's exact test if any expected count is below 5

two_by_two.run:
stats.chi2_contingency(t, correction=False)

# small expected counts
stats.fisher_exact(t)

cross.c:
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import Table2x2
tb = Table2x2(t)
tb.test_nominal_association()
tb.oddsratio_confint()
cross.why: The Pearson chi-square should match scipy's uncorrected statistic exactly.

two_by_two.report: Risk difference, risk ratio, or odds ratio with 95% CI. Use the one the design supports: no risk ratios from case–control samples.
two_by_two.watch: scipy applies Yates' continuity correction to 2×2 tables by default. Decide once and set it explicitly.

chi_sq_indep.name: Chi-square test of independence
chi_sq_indep.when: Two categorical variables with independent observations, such as group by outcome category.

checks.t: Expected counts of 5 or more in about 80% of cells

fb.t: A permutation test of the chi-square statistic when cells are sparse. scipy has no Fisher–Freeman–Halton test.

cross.c:
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import Table
Table(t).test_nominal_association()
cross.why: Second implementation. The statistic and p-value should match.

chi_sq_indep.post: Adjusted standardized residuals per cell: Table(t).standardized_resids.

logistic.name: Logistic regression
logistic.when: A binary outcome with a continuous predictor or several predictors, independent observations.

checks.t: Roughly 10 or more events per parameter
No perfect separation. Huge coefficients and SEs are the symptom
Continuous predictors linear in the logit: try splines
Predictors not too collinear

fb.t: Firth's penalized logistic regression for separation or rare events (firthlogist package).

logistic.run: m = smf.logit('y ~ age + C(group) + x', df).fit()

cross.c:
smf.glm('y ~ age + C(group) + x', df,
        family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit()
cross.why: Logit and binomial GLM are the same model fitted two ways. Coefficients should match to many decimals.

logistic.watch: If the goal is prediction rather than testing an effect, this belongs in a modeling workflow with penalized fits and cross-validated AUC, not a hypothesis test.

stuart_maxwell.name: Stuart–Maxwell test
stuart_maxwell.when: A categorical outcome with three or more levels measured twice on the same subjects (marginal homogeneity).

checks.t: Square table with the same categories at both times

cross.c: SquareTable(t).homogeneity(method='bhapkar')
cross.why: Bhapkar's test targets the same hypothesis and is asymptotically equivalent.

nominal_gee.name: Nominal GEE
nominal_gee.when: An unordered categorical outcome measured repeatedly or within clusters.

checks.t: Enough clusters for robust standard errors
Every category reasonably populated

cross.c: smf.mnlogit('y ~ time + group', df).fit()
cross.why: The naive multinomial fit ignores clustering. Directions should agree; its standard errors will be too small.

nominal_gee.report: Odds ratios against the reference category, with robust CIs.

chi_gof.name: Chi-square goodness-of-fit
chi_gof.when: One categorical variable compared with an expected distribution.

checks.t: Expected counts of 5 or more per category

fb.t: An exact multinomial test when counts are small.

cross.c: stats.power_divergence(observed, expected, lambda_='log-likelihood')
cross.why: The G-test answers the same question. Results should be close in large samples.

mnlogit.name: Multinomial logistic regression
mnlogit.when: An unordered categorical outcome with three or more levels and predictors.

checks.t: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: drop one category and see whether the others shift
Enough observations in every category

cross.c:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
cross.why: The unpenalized fit has the same likelihood but a different parameterization. Compare predicted probabilities, not coefficients.

mnlogit.report: Relative risk ratios (exponentiated coefficients) against the reference category.

gee_poisson.name: Poisson GEE
gee_poisson.when: A count outcome measured repeatedly or within clusters, such as monthly ED visits per patient.

checks.t: Exposure time included as an offset
Enough clusters for robust standard errors
Working correlation chosen

gee_poisson.run:
smf.gee('visits ~ time + group', 'id', df,
        family=sm.families.Poisson(),
        cov_struct=sm.cov_struct.Exchangeable(),
        offset=np.log(df['months'])).fit()

cross.c:
smf.gee('visits ~ time + group', 'id', df,
        family=sm.families.Poisson(),
        cov_struct=sm.cov_struct.Independence(),
        offset=np.log(df['months'])).fit()
cross.why: Robust standard errors should be stable across working correlations.

poisson_2indep.name: Two-sample rate comparison
poisson_2indep.when: Compare event rates between two groups, accounting for different follow-up time.

checks.t: Events within a person roughly independent. Otherwise expect overdispersion

fb.t: Negative binomial regression if the counts are overdispersed.

poisson_2indep.run:
from statsmodels.stats.rates import test_poisson_2indep
test_poisson_2indep(count1, exposure1, count2, exposure2, method='score')

cross.c:
test_poisson_2indep(count1, exposure1, count2, exposure2,
                    method='exact-cond')
cross.why: The conditional exact test should agree closely unless counts are small.

poisson_reg.name: Poisson or negative binomial regression
poisson_reg.when: A count outcome with predictors, optionally with an exposure offset.

checks.t: Dispersion near 1. Well above 1 means negative binomial
Observed zeros close to the number the model predicts

fb.t: A zero-inflated model if there are far more zeros than predicted.

poisson_reg.run:
m = smf.glm('y ~ age + C(group)', df, family=sm.families.Poisson(),
            offset=np.log(df['exposure'])).fit()

# overdispersed
nb = smf.negativebinomial('y ~ age + C(group)', df,
                          exposure=df['exposure']).fit()

cross.c:
# quasi-Poisson: same estimates, SEs scaled by dispersion
smf.glm('y ~ age + C(group)', df, family=sm.families.Poisson(),
        offset=np.log(df['exposure'])).fit(scale='X2')
cross.why: If negative binomial and quasi-Poisson disagree sharply on inference, look at the mean–variance relationship.

zip.name: Zero-inflated count model
zip.when: Counts with more zeros than Poisson or negative binomial predicts, and a plausible reason for structural zeros, such as never-users.

checks.t: A real zero-generating process exists. That's a design question, not a statistical one
Clearly better than plain negative binomial

fb.t: A hurdle model (statsmodels HurdleCountModel) if zeros and positive counts come from separate processes.

zip.run:
from statsmodels.discrete.count_model import ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomialP
ZeroInflatedNegativeBinomialP(y, X, exog_infl=X_infl,
                              inflation='logit').fit()

cross.c: sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit().aic
cross.why: If the zero-inflated model doesn't clearly beat plain negative binomial, the extra zeros may just be overdispersion.

zip.report: Rate ratios for the count part; odds ratios for the zero part.

km_logrank.name: Kaplan–Meier with log-rank test
km_logrank.when: Compare time to event between groups, without adjustment, with censoring.

checks.t: Censoring unrelated to the outcome. That's a design question
Curves don't cross. Crossing curves sap the log-rank test's power

fb.t: Restricted mean survival time when curves cross (lifelines restricted_mean_survival_time).

km_logrank.run:
from statsmodels.duration.survfunc import SurvfuncRight, survdiff
sf = SurvfuncRight(df['time'], df['event'])
chisq, p = survdiff(df['time'], df['event'], df['group'])

cross.c:
from lifelines.statistics import logrank_test
logrank_test(t_a, t_b, event_observed_A=e_a, event_observed_B=e_b)
cross.why: Second implementation of the same test. The chi-square should match.

km_logrank.report: Median survival per group with CI; survival at fixed time points.

cox.name: Cox proportional hazards
cox.when: Time to event with covariates, to estimate hazard ratios.

checks.t: Proportional hazards. Plot Schoenfeld residuals against time; statsmodels has no formal test
Roughly 10 or more events per parameter
Continuous covariates entered in a sensible functional form

fb.t: Stratify on the variable that breaks proportional hazards, or model a time-varying effect.

cox.run:
res = smf.phreg('time ~ age + C(group)', df, status=df['event'],
                ties='efron').fit()

cross.c:
from lifelines import CoxPHFitter
cph = CoxPHFitter().fit(d, duration_col='time', event_col='event')
cph.check_assumptions(d)
cross.why: lifelines uses Efron ties by default; statsmodels uses Breslow. Set ties='efron' or the two won't match.

competing.name: Competing risks analysis
competing.when: More than one event type can end follow-up, such as death before readmission.

checks.t: Estimand chosen: cause-specific hazards for etiology, cumulative incidence for prognosis

fb.t: Fine–Gray subdistribution hazards. Not available in statsmodels or lifelines.

competing.run:
# cumulative incidence
from lifelines import AalenJohansenFitter
ajf = AalenJohansenFitter().fit(df['time'], df['event_type'],
                                event_of_interest=1)

# cause-specific hazard: competing events treated as censored
smf.phreg('time ~ age + C(group)', df,
          status=(df['event_type'] == 1).astype(int)).fit()

cross.c:
from statsmodels.duration.survfunc import SurvfuncRight
naive = SurvfuncRight(df['time'], (df['event_type'] == 1).astype(int))
cross.why: One minus naive Kaplan–Meier overstates cumulative incidence. The size of the gap shows how much competing risks matter here.

competing.report: Cumulative incidence curves; cause-specific hazard ratios.

cox_cluster.name: Clustered or stratified Cox model
cox_cluster.when: Time to event with subjects nested in sites or families, or a covariate that breaks proportional hazards.

checks.t: Enough clusters for robust standard errors
Robust SEs and frailty models answer different questions. Choose deliberately

cox_cluster.run:
# cluster-robust standard errors
smf.phreg('time ~ age + C(group)', df, status=df['event']).fit(groups=df['site'])

# stratify on a non-proportional covariate
smf.phreg('time ~ age + C(group)', df, status=df['event'],
          strata=df['stage']).fit()

cross.c:
CoxPHFitter().fit(d, duration_col='time', event_col='event',
                  cluster_col='site')
cross.why: lifelines' cluster-robust standard errors should be close to statsmodels'.

manova.name: MANOVA
manova.when: Compare groups on several continuous outcomes at once, such as a panel of related lab values.

checks.t: Residuals roughly multivariate normal
Similar covariance matrices across groups. Box's M is in pingouin
Outcomes correlated, but not redundant

fb.t: Rely on Pillai's trace, the most robust of the four statistics.

manova.run:
from statsmodels.multivariate.manova import MANOVA
MANOVA.from_formula('y1 + y2 + y3 ~ group', df).mv_test()

cross.c:
res = MANOVA.from_formula('y1 + y2 + y3 ~ group', df).mv_test()
res.results['group']['stat']
cross.why: All four statistics usually agree. If Pillai's trace and Wilks' λ disagree, assumptions are likely violated; trust Pillai.

manova.report: Pillai's trace; partial η²; follow-up univariate ANOVAs with correction.

mancova.name: MANCOVA
mancova.when: Several continuous outcomes compared between groups, adjusted for covariates.

checks.t: Residuals roughly multivariate normal
Similar covariance matrices across groups
No group × covariate interaction

mancova.run:
from statsmodels.multivariate.manova import MANOVA
MANOVA.from_formula('y1 + y2 ~ C(group) + age + baseline', df).mv_test()

cross.why: Univariate ANCOVAs don't replace the joint test, but a joint effect with no univariate signal at all deserves a closer look.

mancova.report: Pillai's trace; adjusted group differences per outcome.

mv_reg.name: Multivariate multiple regression
mv_reg.when: Predict several continuous outcomes from the same set of continuous predictors.

checks.t: Residuals roughly multivariate normal
Predictors not too collinear

mv_reg.run:
MANOVA.from_formula('y1 + y2 ~ x1 + x2', df).mv_test()  # joint tests
fits = {y: smf.ols(f'{y} ~ x1 + x2', df).fit() for y in ['y1', 'y2']}

cross.c: B = np.linalg.lstsq(X, Y, rcond=None)[0]
cross.why: Coefficients are identical to the separate OLS fits. Only the joint tests differ.

mv_reg.report: Coefficients per outcome with CIs; a multivariate test per predictor.

factor_sem.name: Factor analysis or SEM
factor_sem.when: The outcomes are items of a scale or indicators of an underlying construct, such as questionnaire domains.

checks.t: Exploratory or confirmatory. That's a design decision
Enough subjects per item
Items correlated enough to factor (KMO, Bartlett)

factor_sem.run:
from statsmodels.multivariate.factor import Factor
res = Factor(items, n_factor=3, method='ml').fit()
res.rotate('varimax')

cross.c:
import semopy
m = semopy.Model(desc)
m.fit(df)
semopy.calc_stats(m)
cross.why: Exploratory loadings should resemble the structure you'd specify confirmatorily. Fit indices tell you whether it holds.

factor_sem.watch: This is model building, not test selection. Flag it and hand it to a person.

pearson.name: Pearson correlation
pearson.when: Linear association between two continuous variables.

checks.t: Linear relationship. Plot it first
No single point driving the coefficient
Roughly bivariate normal, for the p-value and CI

fb.t: Spearman rank correlation.

cross.c: np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]
cross.why: The coefficient must match exactly.

point_biserial.name: Point-biserial correlation
point_biserial.when: Association between a binary variable and a continuous one.

checks.t: The continuous variable roughly normal within each group
Similar variances in the two groups

fb.t: Mann–Whitney U.

cross.c: stats.ttest_ind(x[binary == 1], x[binary == 0], equal_var=True)
cross.why: Mathematically identical to Student's t-test. Same p-value.

partial_corr.name: Partial correlation
partial_corr.when: Association between two continuous variables after removing the effect of one or more others.

checks.t: Linear relationships with the covariates
Residuals roughly normal

partial_corr.run:
import pingouin as pg
pg.partial_corr(df, x='x', y='y', covar=['age', 'bmi'])

cross.c:
rx = smf.ols('x ~ age + bmi', df).fit().resid
ry = smf.ols('y ~ age + bmi', df).fit().resid
stats.pearsonr(rx, ry)
cross.why: Correlating residuals gives the same coefficient. Its p-value uses too many degrees of freedom, so trust pingouin's.

cohen_kappa.name: Cohen's kappa
cohen_kappa.when: Two raters assign categories to the same items. Use weighted kappa for ordinal ratings.

checks.t: Both raters use the same set of categories
Kappa drops when one category dominates. Report raw agreement too

cohen_kappa.run:
from statsmodels.stats.inter_rater import cohens_kappa, to_table
table, _ = to_table(np.column_stack([r1, r2]))
cohens_kappa(table, wt='quadratic')  # omit wt for nominal ratings

cross.c:
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
cohen_kappa_score(r1, r2, weights='quadratic')
cross.why: Point estimates should match. statsmodels adds the standard error and CI.

cohen_kappa.report: κ with 95% CI, plus percent agreement.

fleiss_kappa.name: Fleiss' kappa
fleiss_kappa.when: Three or more raters assign categories to the same items.

checks.t: Every item rated by the same number of raters. If not, use Krippendorff's α

fleiss_kappa.run:
from statsmodels.stats.inter_rater import fleiss_kappa, aggregate_raters
counts, _ = aggregate_raters(ratings)  # ratings: items × raters
fleiss_kappa(counts)

cross.c:
import krippendorff
krippendorff.alpha(reliability_data=ratings.T,
                   level_of_measurement='nominal')
cross.why: Krippendorff's α is close to Fleiss' κ for complete nominal data, and also handles missing ratings.

bland_altman.name: Bland–Altman analysis
bland_altman.when: Two methods measure the same continuous quantity, such as a new device against a reference.

checks.t: Differences roughly normal
No proportional bias: regress differences on means

fb.t: Log-transform, or report ratio limits, if differences grow with magnitude.

bland_altman.run:
d = m1 - m2
bias, sd = d.mean(), d.std(ddof=1)
loa = (bias - 1.96 * sd, bias + 1.96 * sd)

cross.c: sm.graphics.mean_diff_plot(m1, m2)
cross.why: The plot draws its own bias and limit lines. They should sit exactly where the hand-computed values say.

bland_altman.report: Bias and 95% limits of agreement, each with a CI.
bland_altman.watch: Correlation measures association, not agreement. Two methods can correlate at 0.99 and still disagree clinically.

icc.name: Intraclass correlation (ICC)
icc.when: Reliability of continuous ratings across raters, or across repeated measurements.

checks.t: Form chosen: one-way or two-way, random or fixed raters, agreement or consistency, single or average
Residuals roughly normal

icc.run:
import pingouin as pg
pg.intraclass_corr(data=df, targets='patient', raters='rater', ratings='score')

cross.c:
# ICC(2,1) from two-way ANOVA mean squares
m = smf.ols('score ~ C(patient) + C(rater)', df).fit()
sm.stats.anova_lm(m)
cross.why: Plug the mean squares into the Shrout–Fleiss formula. It should reproduce pingouin's ICC2 row.

icc.report: ICC form named explicitly, such as ICC(2,1) absolute agreement, with 95% CI.
icc.watch: Six ICC forms give different numbers on the same data. The design decides the form; the tool should ask, not guess.

diag_binary.name: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values
diag_binary.when: A binary test result compared with a gold-standard diagnosis.

checks.t: Gold standard applied to everyone, not only to test positives
PPV and NPV depend on prevalence. Skip them in case–control samples

diag_binary.run:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(truth, test).ravel()
sens, spec = tp / (tp + fn), tn / (tn + fp)
proportion_confint(tp, tp + fn, method='wilson')

cross.c: pd.crosstab(truth, test)
cross.why: An independent tally catches label-encoding mistakes about which class is positive, the most common bug here.

diag_binary.report: Sensitivity and specificity with Wilson CIs; LR+ and LR−.

roc_auc.name: ROC curve and AUC
roc_auc.when: A continuous score or predicted probability compared with a binary gold standard.

checks.t: Positive class defined explicitly
No CI in sklearn. Use a stratified bootstrap or DeLong

roc_auc.run:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve
auc = roc_auc_score(y, score)
fpr, tpr, thr = roc_curve(y, score)

cross.c:
u = stats.mannwhitneyu(score[y == 1], score[y == 0]).statistic
u / ((y == 1).sum() * (y == 0).sum())
cross.why: AUC equals the Mann–Whitney U divided by n₁n₀. They must match exactly; if not, the positive class is flipped.

roc_auc.report: AUC with 95% CI; sensitivity and specificity at a pre-specified threshold.
roc_auc.watch: A threshold chosen on the same data you report it on is optimistic. Fix it in advance or validate it.

delong.name: DeLong test for paired AUCs
delong.when: Two scores evaluated on the same patients: is one AUC larger?

checks.t: Same patients and the same outcome labels for both scores
Not a model compared with the same model plus one marker

delong.run:
# not in scipy, statsmodels or sklearn: write it once
# (fast DeLong, Sun and Xu 2014) and unit-test it
auc_a, auc_b, p = delong_paired(y, score_a, score_b)

cross.c:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
diffs = []
for _ in range(2000):
    i = rng.integers(0, len(y), len(y))
    diffs.append(roc_auc_score(y[i], a[i]) - roc_auc_score(y[i], b[i]))
np.percentile(diffs, [2.5, 97.5])
cross.why: A paired bootstrap of the AUC difference should give a similar CI. Use it to validate your DeLong implementation.

delong.xcall: paired bootstrap of the AUC difference
delong.report: AUC difference with 95% CI and p-value.
delong.watch: Don't use it to test whether adding a marker to a nested model improves AUC; that comparison is known to be invalid. Test the marker's coefficient instead.
